test_title: PYST 74: RRB Group D - GS (Held On: 30 Dec, 2025 Shift 2)
subject: general
question: During an experiment, a cell is damaged and its lysosomes burst, releasing digestive enzymes into the cytoplasm. What is most likely to happen next?

options.text: The mitochondria will produce more energy.
The cell will grow in size.
The cell will destroy itself and die.

solution:
The correct answer is __**The cell will destroy itself and die**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Lysosomes** are **membrane-bound** organelles found in almost all **eukaryotic cells**. They are known as the **"suicide bags"** of the cell because of their unique function in cell death.
 
• These organelles contain powerful **digestive enzymes** called **acid hydrolases**, which are capable of breaking down **proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, and carbohydrates**.
 
• When a cell is **damaged** or undergoes significant **stress**, the membrane of the **lysosome** can **burst**, releasing its enzymatic contents directly into the **cytoplasm**.
 
• Once released, these **enzymes** begin to digest the **cell's own components** (organelles and structural proteins). This biological process of self-digestion is called **autolysis**.
 
• As a result of this **uncontrolled digestion**, the cell is unable to maintain its **structural integrity** or **metabolic functions**, leading to the **death of the cell**. *Hence, the statement that the cell will destroy itself and die is correct.*
 
• The other processes mentioned, such as **mitochondrial energy production** (Option 1) or **nuclear division** (Option 4), require a stable and healthy **cytoplasmic environment**. The presence of destructive **enzymes** inhibits these vital functions. *Hence, these statements are incorrect.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Discovery:** The **lysosome** was discovered and named by the **Belgian cytologist Christian de Duve** in **1955**, for which he later received a **Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine** in **1974**.
 
• **Enzyme Environment:** The **enzymes** within a lysosome work best in **acidic conditions**, typically maintaining a **pH of about 4.5 to 5.0** inside the organelle. The **cytoplasm**, by contrast, has a near-neutral **pH of about 7.2**.
 
• **Formation:** Lysosomes are formed by the **budding off** from the **Golgi apparatus**. The **hydrolytic enzymes** they contain are originally synthesized in the **Rough Endoplasmic Reticulum (RER)**.
 
• **Functions:** Beyond self-destruction, they serve critical roles in **waste removal**, **autophagy** (digesting old cell parts to recycle materials), and **phagocytosis** (digesting foreign invaders like **bacteria** or **viruses**).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Lysosomal Storage Diseases (LSDs):** If the **lysosomal enzymes** are missing or **malfunctioning** due to genetic mutations, substances that should be broken down accumulate in the cell. Examples include **Tay-Sachs disease**, **Gaucher's disease**, and **Pompe disease**.
 
• **Autolysis vs. Apoptosis:** **Autolysis** is usually a **pathological** process occurring after cell injury. In contrast, **apoptosis** is a **genetically programmed** and orderly form of cell death used during **embryonic development** (like the removal of webbing between fingers) and to eliminate **cancerous cells**.
 
• **Location:** While primarily associated with **animal cells**, lysosome-like **vacuoles** perform similar digestive functions in **plant cells** and **fungi**.
</ul
